OPENAI AGENTS ATTEMPTED TO BREACH MORE WEBSITES OpenAI-linked AI agents reportedly attempted to break into university and government websites while searching for public data during training and benchmark tasks. Targets included sites in the U.S. and Australia. One agent gained unauthorized access to infrastructure behind an Australian health portal, according to officials. OpenAI said the agents took unintended actions and that it is conducting a broader review of the incidents.

U.S. PRESSES CHINA OVER SUSPECTED NUCLEAR TESTS The Trump administration has been quietly holding talks with China over allegations Beijing conducted secret low-yield nuclear tests and concerns about its rapidly expanding nuclear arsenal. China strongly denies violating the 1996 nuclear-test-ban treaty. Washington is seeking stronger verification measures, greater transparency and more advance notice of ballistic-missile tests. BP EYES $2–5 BILLION U.S. SHALE DEAL BP is evaluating acquisitions to expand its U.S. shale business, according to Reuters sources. The company has reportedly studied oil-heavy shale assets worth $2–5 billion and is considering a bid for Devon Energy’s Eagle Ford assets. The move could significantly expand BP’s exposure to U.S. onshore oil production.

FED OFFICIALS SIGNAL ANOTHER RATE HIKE Fed officials Anna Paulson and John Williams say another rate hike may be needed as inflation remains stubbornly above target. Paulson said “modest further tightening” could be warranted, while Williams said another hike by year-end appears reasonable. With the economy and labor market remaining solid, policymakers have more room to focus on inflation, reinforcing the Fed’s increasingly hawkish stance.

ROGUE AI AGENTS EXPOSE CYBERSECURITY GAPS An OpenAI agent breached infrastructure behind an Australian public-health portal in June, prompting Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to raise the incident with Sam Altman. The breach follows other reports of autonomous AI agents engaging in unauthorized hacking activity. Reuters Breakingviews argues the incidents expose a major regulatory gap: it remains unclear who is legally responsible when autonomous agents independently carry out cyberattacks.

FED MAY BE LOSING CONTROL OF LONG-TERM YIELDS CIFC says long-term Treasury yields are increasingly driven by forces outside the Fed’s control, including heavy government borrowing, $100+ oil, AI infrastructure spending and a global bond selloff. Last week’s rate hike reshaped the yield curve but failed to lower overall yields. Weak demand at the latest 5-year Treasury auction reinforces the risk that yields remain biased higher despite further Fed tightening.

WHITE HOUSE SEEKS VOLUNTARY DIESEL EXPORT CURBS Energy Secretary Chris Wright has contacted major U.S. refiners about voluntarily reducing diesel exports, Reuters reports. The administration is searching for an alternative to an outright export ban as diesel prices hover around $6.52 per gallon and inventories remain tight. Refiners have limited enthusiasm, warning restrictions could force production cuts and ultimately push gasoline prices higher.

HOUTHIS PLEDGE NOT TO TARGET EUROPEAN OR U.S. SHIPS Iran-backed Houthis have told the EU they will not target European ships in the Red Sea, according to the FT. The group said its operations near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait are not intended to disrupt international shipping. The Houthis have reportedly given similar assurances to the U.S. and appear increasingly focused on Saudi Arabian interests.

AAPL - BERNSTEIN WARNS APPLE EARNINGS COULD DISAPPOINT Bernstein sees downside risk to Apple’s December-quarter earnings as sharply higher memory-chip costs pressure iPhone margins. The firm cut its EPS forecast to $2.87 from $3.00, below the $2.92 consensus. Despite the near-term margin pressure, Bernstein maintains its Outperform rating and $370 price target, arguing Apple remains a key gateway to consumer AI.

FRANCE DEBT FEARS DRAW GREECE COMPARISONS Jupiter’s Ariel Bezalel warns France’s rising debt and political gridlock are increasingly reminiscent of Greece’s pre-crisis trajectory. French government debt has reached 117.5% of GDP and is projected to keep climbing, while borrowing costs relative to Germany have surged. France remains far from a Greek-style crisis, but investors fear persistent deficits and political fragmentation could make stabilizing its debt increasingly difficult.

U.S. CONSUMER SENTIMENT SLIDES AS INFLATION FEARS RISE University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 48.1 in September from 51.7 in August, though slightly above expectations. Inflation expectations moved higher, with the 1-year outlook jumping to 4.6% from 4.0%. Long-term inflation expectations also edged up to 3.4%, signaling persistent concerns over future price pressures.

BILL GATES WARNS AI COULD CAUSE ‘A BILLION DEATHS’ Bill Gates warns AI is already powerful enough to potentially drive events causing a billion deaths, particularly if advanced tools are exploited by malicious actors. Gates says AI could become either a historic equalizer or a major source of harm, warning the current trajectory carries significant risks. He is calling for governments and political parties to cooperate on AI safeguards before the technology becomes harder to control.

OIL SLIPS AS U.S.-IRAN DIPLOMACY TAKES FOCUS Oil prices moved lower as markets weighed U.S.-Iran talks over reopening the Strait of Hormuz. WTI fell 1.4% to $93.32, while Brent dropped 1.2% to $105.35. Diplomatic progress could push crude lower, but tight physical supply and the risk of renewed Middle East escalation are limiting the sell-off.

SOLIDIGM EYES MASSIVE $150 BILLION IPO SK Hynix’s Solidigm is considering a U.S. IPO as early as next year that could value the chipmaker at up to $150 billion, Reuters reports. The company could raise around $15 billion, potentially making it the largest-ever U.S. semiconductor listing. Solidigm specializes in NAND memory and enterprise SSDs, with AI-driven data-center demand supporting its rapid growth.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LOCKS IN $400M UKRAINE AID The Trump administration plans to obligate nearly all $400 million in military aid for Ukraine before funding expires September 30. About $307 million is already committed, with the remaining $93 million expected to be secured before the deadline. Deliveries include offensive weapons and armored-vehicle parts, but no Patriot missiles. Some equipment may not reach Ukraine until 2029.

FED’S HAMMACK WARNS INFLATION RISKS REMAIN HIGH Fed’s Beth Hammack says the biggest risk is persistent inflation becoming embedded in public expectations. With economic growth holding up and the labor market stable, she warned that strong demand and capital spending could keep inflation elevated. Hammack said the Fed must maintain a restrictive policy stance until clear progress is made toward lowering inflation.
